topic: Religion, Philosophy & Ethics: The Existence of God
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Hindu deities are often understood as manifestations of one Brahman
items.claim: How does Hindu theology relate the many gods to Brahman?

options.text: Each god is wholly separate and independent

Many Hindus understand the gods as manifestations (devas) of one ultimate reality (Brahman) — though the relationship varies between traditions; the Rig Veda (1.164.46) says 'Truth is one; sages call it by many names'
There is only one god — Brahma alone

items.reveal:
The Trimurti (Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer) is one classical mapping of cosmic functions.

Vaishnavism centres on Vishnu and his avatars (Rama, Krishna). Shaivism centres on Shiva. Shaktism centres on Devi/Shakti (the divine feminine — Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati). Each tradition may treat its chosen deity as supreme.

The term 'henotheism' (worshipping one god while acknowledging others) was coined by Max Müller in the 19th century specifically to describe Vedic religion.
items.why: Calling Hinduism polytheistic or monotheistic both miss the structure. The 'many manifestations of one' framework is philosophically distinct — and shapes how Hindus actually relate to images and shrines.

items.title: Jihad means 'struggle' — and has a greater inner meaning
items.claim: What is the classical Islamic distinction between greater and lesser jihad?

options.text: Greater jihad is large-scale war; lesser jihad is small skirmishes

A widely cited hadith distinguishes the 'lesser jihad' (armed struggle in defence of the community) from the 'greater jihad' (the inner struggle against one's own ego) — though the hadith's authenticity is debated by some scholars
Jihad means only armed warfare; it has no inner meaning
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Scholars including Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and modern critics question the hadith's authenticity. But the inner-struggle understanding is found independently in Sufi traditions and in mainstream piety.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: The Five Pillars have a canonical order — beginning with Shahada
items.claim: What is the standard Sunni order of the Five Pillars of Islam?

options.text: Shahada (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (almsgiving, 2.5% of accumulated wealth), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca, once if able)

items.reveal:
The Hadith of Gabriel (recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) lists the Pillars in this order. The Shahada is the doorway — 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God'.

Shia Islam (Twelver tradition) frames obligations differently. They recognise the practices but as part of the Furu al-Din (Ten Ancillaries of the Religion), alongside jihad, enjoining good and forbidding wrong, tawalla (love of the household of the Prophet) and tabarra (disassociation from enemies).

Zakat is calculated annually on accumulated wealth above a threshold (nisab); Sawm requires no food, drink or marital relations from dawn (fajr) to sunset (maghrib) during Ramadan.
items.why: Religious practice has specific structure. Treating the Pillars as a vague list of good acts misses the theological logic — faith first, then prayer, then social action.
